description: WifiHaven websocket router transport (#1846, epic #1023): server-side health for the persistent /api/router/ws endpoint. Panels target only the series the API actually emits today — router_ws_connections_active (RouterWsRegistry) and router_ws_frames_total{op,direction,result} (RouterWsRoutes demux). The REST transport stays the fallback; until the agent ws client (#1848) ships these read 0/flat. Push-on-change health (router_ws_policy_push_total) lands with #1849. Per-ws-message-process latency (router_ws_message_duration_seconds, #2168) is the ws analog of http_request_duration_seconds — it must land before the #1023 prod cutover / #1850 poll removal so slow-op regressions on the socket stay visible. router_ws_connections_superseded_total (#2561) counts half-open sockets evicted on reconnect — the residual signal behind the connections gauge. Labels are bounded enums only per the §4 cardinality firewall. datasource/env are templated for per-environment view.

panels.title: Websocket connections active (#1846)
panels.description: router_ws_connections_active — live count of open /api/router/ws channels, recomputed from the registry on every register/deregister so it is a pure function of registry state. #2561: a re-connect for a router that is already present now supersedes (evicts + shuts down) the stale channel, so the gauge is bounded by the number of connected ROUTERS and can no longer drift upward when a socket goes half-open without a close handshake — it read 2 with one router connected before that fix. Pair with "WS stale-connection supersedes" for the half-open rate this now absorbs. The single "how many routers are on the ws transport right now?" signal.

panels.title: Websocket frame rate by op/direction/result (#1846)
panels.description: sum by (op, direction, result) (rate(router_ws_frames_total[5m])) — frame throughput across the {op,payload} demux. dir ∈ {in,out}; result ∈ {ok,reject,unknown_op}. A rising result=reject share means agents are sending frames the server rejects (the ws analog of a REST 4xx); result=unknown_op is the forward-compat counter for frames whose op the server does not recognize (design §1.3).

panels.title: Websocket frames by op (rate)
panels.description: sum by (op) (rate(router_ws_frames_total[5m])) — total frame rate per logical channel (hello/usage/events/metrics/ping/pong/ack). Lets an operator see which flows dominate the socket and confirm heartbeats (ping/pong) are ticking.

panels.title: Websocket reject + unknown_op rate
panels.description: sum by (op) (rate(router_ws_frames_total{result=~"reject|unknown_op"}[5m])) — the error surface of the transport isolated. Steady non-zero here is the first sign agents and server disagree on the wire (a bad payload, or an op one side hasn't shipped yet).

panels.title: Agent ws link state by router (ws_state) (#1848)
panels.description: max by (router_id) (ws_state) — the wifihaven-ws sidecar's link gauge folded into the agent /metrics push: 1 = a live websocket to the API, 0 = disconnected (running on the HTTP fallback path). One series per router_id (bounded fleet dimension). Complements the server-side router_ws_connections_active gauge.

panels.title: Agent ws connect outcomes by result (#1848)
panels.description: sum by (result) (rate(ws_connect_total[5m])) — reconnect health from the agent side. result ∈ {ok, upgrade_fail, auth_fail, timeout}. Rising auth_fail = the bearer token is rejected at upgrade; upgrade_fail/timeout = a proxy mangling Upgrade or an unreachable endpoint (the agent falls back to HTTP, §3.1).

panels.title: Agent ws HTTP-fallback events by result (#1848)
panels.description: sum by (result) (rate(ws_fallback_total[5m])) — how often the agent crossed the transport boundary. to_http: the socket was down past ws_fallback_after and the agent resumed HTTP polling; back_to_ws: the socket re-established. A high to_http without matching back_to_ws means the fleet is stuck on HTTP — do NOT arm any poll-deprecation (§3.1/§3.2).

panels.title: Agent ws frame throughput sent/recv by op (#1848)
panels.description: sum by (op) (rate(ws_frames_sent_total[5m])) and ws_frames_recv_total — agent-side frame throughput. sent op ∈ {usage, events, ping}; recv op ∈ {policy, ack, pong, unknown}. A pushed policy shows as recv op=policy (server push is #1849); usage/events sent are the outbound spool drain.

panels.title: Policy snapshot builds: computed vs cache_hit (#1849 / #1512)
panels.description: sum by (result) (rate(policy_snapshot_build_total[5m])) — proves the computed-snapshot cache is working. result=computed is an actual ~500ms PolicyService rebuild (the #1512 cost); result=cache_hit is a poll/ws-fanout served from the cache without rebuilding. Once the reconcile ticker keeps the cache warm, cache_hit should dominate and computed should track the policy-change/tick rate (≈1 per snapshotCacheRefreshSeconds), NOT the per-poll-per-router rate. A computed rate that scales with router count means the cache is not being read.

panels.title: WS policy push fan-out by result (#1849)
panels.description:
sum by (result) (rate(router_ws_policy_push_total[5m])) — health of the push-on-change fan-out. result=ok is a policy frame handed to a connected channel; result=channel_closed is a send that failed against a racing disconnect (the channel is dropped). A sustained channel_closed share suggests routers are churning their sockets.

#2630 added two REFUSED-delivery results, both of which should read flat ZERO. result=household_mismatch: a push was handed a snapshot built for a household other than the receiving router's, and nothing was sent. Since #2630 the change fan-out cannot even produce a frame for another household, so this can only fire on the first-policy-on-connect path and means a caller bug — any non-zero value is a caught cross-tenant policy delivery and is actionable. result=unregistered: a first-policy push for a router with no registry entry, so its household could not be established and nothing was sent; a rate here means a caller is pushing before registering and that router gets no first policy at all.

Also note #2630 changed what ok COUNTS: attempts at recipients, and a router in another household is no longer a recipient. The step down in ok at that deploy is the leak stopping, not a regression.

panels.title: Policy poll suppressed while ws healthy (#2037)
panels.description: sum by (reason) (rate(policy_poll_skipped_total[5m])) — the agent-side dormancy gate (design §3.1). When ws is enabled AND its health sentinel is fresh (within ws_fallback_after), the agent's 5 s HTTP GET /api/router/policy poll goes dormant (reason=ws_healthy) — the push channel is the live transport, so the server stops recomputing the snapshot per poll (#1512). This is the agent-side complement of the 'Policy snapshot builds: computed vs cache_hit' panel above: a climbing skip rate on ws routers alongside a flat snapshot_poll_total is the load win of enabling ws being realized. A skip rate that drops to 0 while ws_state stays 1 means the dormancy gate regressed (poll running despite a healthy link).

panels.title: WS message process latency p50/p95/p99 (#2168)
panels.description: histogram_quantile over router_ws_message_duration_seconds_bucket — per-ws-message-process latency (decode → handle → ack inbound, policy-push send outbound), the ws analog of http_request_duration_seconds. Reuses the HTTP latency buckets so a ws op's latency is directly comparable to the REST endpoint it replaced across the #1023 cutover. Once the poll is removed (#1850) this is the ONLY latency signal for router operations — a p99 climb here is the ws-transport equivalent of the /api/usage/traffic regression per-endpoint metrics caught.

panels.title: WS message process p95 latency by op/direction (#2168)
panels.description: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, op, direction) (rate(router_ws_message_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) — per-op p95, so a single slow logical channel (e.g. a usage ingest that got expensive) is visible even when the aggregate looks fine. op ∈ {usage,events,metrics,ping,pong,hello,policy,unknown}, direction ∈ {in,out} — bounded enums, no per-mac/router dimension.

panels.title: WS push→apply latency p50/p95/p99 (#2229)
panels.description: histogram_quantile over ws_push_apply_latency_seconds_bucket — time from the sidecar persisting a server-pushed policy snapshot to the agent applying it to the enforcement plane (nft). Event-driven since #2229 (the sidecar writes a trigger the agent reads every heartbeat tick); should sit in low single-digit seconds, dominated by nft load, no longer gated by the dnsmasq restart. Flat/0 until agents on ws receive a push.

panels.title: WS frame reassembly + overflow (#2268)
panels.description: rate of router_ws_reassembly_total / spa_ws_reassembly_total by result. completed = a multi-frame message the server rejoined (an intermediary — Render's edge — fragmented it at ~4 KiB; the router→server transport relies on this reassembly, mirror of #1959). overflow = a peer streamed past the 1 MiB cap and the connection was closed — should be flat zero; any sustained non-zero is an oversized/misbehaving sender. spa_* is latent today (browsers reassemble server→browser natively) but shares the reassembler.

panels.title: WS stale-connection supersedes (#2561)
panels.description: rate of router_ws_connections_superseded_total — a router re-connected while the server still held a channel for it, i.e. the previous socket went half-open and its teardown never ran. The registry now evicts + shuts that stale channel down, which is what keeps router_ws_connections_active honest (it read 2 with one router connected before #2561). This counter is the residual signal: it should be low and bursty (a router rebooting / NAT rebind), and a sustained rate means sockets are dying without a close handshake — the routers are churning between ws and the poll fallback even though the connections gauge looks healthy. Unlabelled (a router id would be a fleet-sized dimension).

panels.title: routers.last_etag stamp outcomes (#2619)
panels.description:
rate of router_ws_etag_stamp_total by outcome — the delivery-time write of routers.last_etag that rides every websocket policy push. That column is what the operator's "who is on current policy?" view reads, and until #2619 only the REST poll wrote it; since #2608 made ws the router default the poll goes dormant on a healthy link (#2037), so this push is the only writer for most of the fleet. The stamp is best-effort — a DB failure must not tear down a policy delivery — so nothing else on the push path moves when it breaks, and this series is the only signal.

`ok`: written; should track the policy-push rate.
`error`: the write failed and the column is silently going stale. This is the ALERTABLE series — any sustained rate is actionable.
#2630 RETIRED the `household_mismatch` and `unregistered` outcomes from this series: the household guard moved off the stamp and onto the DELIVERY (router_ws_policy_push_total), which is where the leak actually was — #2619 refused the durable write while the frame still went out. Historically, `household_mismatch` here before the #2630 deploy is the leak’s live blast radius; both outcomes go flat and age out after it.

Bounded 2-value enum; no per-router or per-household label rides it.
